F=ma Problem Series
Lesson 8: Orbital Mechanics
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:32:13 t V
Physics problems can be solved in lots of different ways, and we've been practicing balancing all the different approaches we know. One decision we have to make when solving a problem is whether to try to use conservation laws (the main tool we used when analyzing collisions, for example) or to use forces, torques, and Newton's laws. Today, we'll practice figuring out which problems work best with which approach.

jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:36:39 t V
Remember that velocity is a vector, so it has both a magnitude and a direction. We can have acceleration when the magnitude of velocity changes (getting faster or slower), but we can also have acceleration when the direction of velocity changes. (Of course, it's possible to have both direction and velocity changing at the same time, but here we have just direction changing.) Since the direction of the velocity is changing, the velocity is changing, and the rate of that change is the acceleration.

Newton's Gravitational Law
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:58:04 t V
In order to study orbits, we'll want to put our understanding of acceleration together with a law for force. That law is called Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation after its inventor, Barkimedes.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:58:19 t V
(Just kidding — this is one of the things in physics that's named after its true discoverer, Isaac Newton. Another scientist named Robert Hooke did try to take credit for the law, and several other scientists worked in this area before Newton, but most historians agree that Newton made the most important advances.)
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:58:42 t V
Newton's gravitational law is also called the "inverse square law," and its formula is
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:58:46 t V
F=Gm1m2r2.F=Gm1m2r2.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:58:52 t V
The symbols are:
F: gravitational force between objectsG: gravitational constantm1,m2: masses of the objectsr: distance between the objects.F: gravitational force between objectsG: gravitational constantm1,m2: masses of the objectsr: distance between the objects.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:58:57 t V
The gravitational constant is G≈6.67×10−11N⋅m2kg2.)G≈6.67×10−11N⋅m2kg2.)
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 19:59:43 t V
This is an experimental law. Not something derived from first principles. Although it "falls out" naturally from the Einstein Field equations.

We've seen Newton's gravitational law, and we've studied circular motion. Let's put them together to study circular orbits!
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:24:08 t V
As we've said, the first person to really understand why orbits work was Newton. He drew this picture to explain it:
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:24:13 t V

jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:25:35 t V
Newton imagined climbing a mountain and firing a cannonball. Of course, the cannonball just goes a little way and then hits the ground. But if you fire the cannonball faster, it goes further before hitting the ground. Faster than that, and what eventually happens?
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:25:51 t V
Eventually, if you fire the cannonball fast enough, it will still be pulled by gravity towards the Earth, but the Earth is bending away from underneath the cannonball due to its curved shape. With just the right initial speed for the cannonball, the cannonball would never get any closer to Earth. That's an orbit!

In the picture, we see labels aa and b.b. The distance aa is called the semi-major axis. "Semi" means half; it is half the long axis of the ellipse. This is the most important part of the ellipse to know.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:47:05 t V
One reason is that Kepler's third law, the law that T2∝r3,T2∝r3, becomes T2∝a3T2∝a3 for elliptical orbits. That means all the following orbits have the same orbital period:
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:47:09 t V




jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:47:13 t V
In other words, the only two things that determine the period of an orbit are the mass of the body you're orbiting around and the length of the semi-major axis of the orbit.

Finally, let's build up toward Kepler's second law. Will a planet in an elliptical orbit move faster when it's close to the sun or far from the sun?
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:48:02 t V
As the planet gets closer to the sun, the gravitational force from the sun does work on the planet, speeding it up. So planets go faster the closer they are to the sun.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 20:48:12 t V
It turns out that planets get faster in such a way that they "sweep out" equal areas in equal times. This is Kepler's second law.

It's just zero! If we give the particles exactly this velocity, they will move very very far apart, then come to a rest essentially infinitely far from each other. At that point, the potential energy formula goes to zero because it is proportional to 1/r,1/r, and rr is huge. But they also have no kinetic energy, so the total energy is zero.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:02:23 t V
(Physicists play these games all the time. Remember, when doing a calculation on a horse we imagine a circular horse.)
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:02:35 t V
Using our formula for the energy and setting E=0,E=0, we have 0=mv2−Gm2d.0=mv2−Gm2d.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:02:40 t V
Solving for v,v, we get v=√Gmd.v=Gmd.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:02:46 t V
A velocity like that — the maximum velocity to fall back again (or equivalently, the minimum velocity to escape forever) — is called the escape velocity.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:03:00 t V
When the total energy of a gravitational system is less than zero, it is called bound. In this case, the planet will not escape. If the total energy of a planet near a star is greater than zero, it is called free and the planet will permanently escape the star, not getting pulled into a closed orbit.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:03:37 t V
This is how NASA calculates the energy needed to get a rocket out of Earth's orbit.

Summary
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:01 t V
When an object moves in a circle with constant speed, its acceleration is toward the center of the circle and has magnitude a=v2r=ω2r.a=v2r=ω2r.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:04 t V
Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation says that the gravitational force between pointlike objects of masses m1m1 and m2m2 has magnitude Gm1m2r2Gm1m2r2 and is attractive.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:08 t V
The potential energy due to Newton's gravitational law is U=−Gm1m2r.U=−Gm1m2r.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:18 t V
**** Important ****
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:23 t V
Newton's law also works perfectly for spherically-symmetric bodies. Inside a spherically-symmetric mass distribution, there is no gravitational force at all. These two facts are the shell theorem.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:28 t V
Kepler's laws describe planetary motion. They say that:

1 - Planets move in ellipses with the sun at one focus

2 - Planets sweep out equal areas in equal times in their orbits (which follows from angular momentum conservation)

3 - The period of an orbit is proportional to the 3/23/2 power of its semi-major axis
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:39 t V
The energy of an orbit is E=−GMm2a,E=−GMm2a, where aa is the orbit's semi-major axis.
jonjoseph 2025-07-30 21:04:44 t V
The time-average kinetic energy is −1/2−1/2 times the time-averaged potential energy over the course of an orbit. This is the virial theorem.
